query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of a ductile BCC element, such as vanadium at around 5–10 at%, into NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while maintaining its high-temperature mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent high-temperature mechanical properties (up to 1600 °C) but shows poor ductility at room temperature and has only computationally inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Micro-alloy the NbMoTaW alloy by substituting 5–10 at% of one of the larger refractory elements (e.g., Mo or Ta) with vanadium.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature for ductility, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) tests for strength retention, and exposure to helium ion irradiation at fluences representative of reactor conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice heterogeneity and a refined grain structure with possible formation of nanoscale local ordering or subtle precipitates that do not disrupt the overall BCC stability.
generation.mechanism: The addition of vanadium is expected to increase lattice distortion heterogeneity, which promotes dislocation mobility at low temperatures (thereby improving ductility) and facilitates efficient recombination of irradiation-induced point defects. This micro-alloying also preserves the dominant BCC phase, ensuring that high-temperature strength is retained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the vanadium-doped alloy will show improved room-temperature tensile elongation and a decrease in brittleness, reduced irradiation-induced defect clustering (evidenced by smaller helium bubble sizes and lower defect densities), while its high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) remains comparable.
generation.baseline: Pristine, equal-atomic NbMoTaW that is BCC single-phase with excellent high-temperature performance but limited ductility at room temperature and uncertain irradiation performance.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements apply under room temperature mechanical loading and under helium irradiation conditions typical of reactor environments, with high-temperature performance verified up to approximately 1600 °C. Outside these conditions, the effects of vanadium addition remain to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal vanadium concentration may require fine tuning; there is uncertainty regarding potential adverse interactions under prolonged irradiation or at extreme high temperatures, which must be established by experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys under identical processing conditions: one set of pristine NbMoTaW and one set with 5–10 at% vanadium substitution. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to determine ductility and yield strength, high-temperature mechanical tests (up to 1600 °C) to assess strength retention, and subject samples to controlled helium ion irradiation at reactor-relevant fluences. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to evaluate defect formation, helium bubble size, and phase stability before and after irradiation.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile elongation (% strain to failure) and yield strength
Irradiation-induced defect density and helium bubble size distribution from TEM
Phase identification and lattice parameter stability from XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-doped NbMoTaW does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility or if it exhibits either a degradation in high-temperature strength or an increase in irradiation-induced defect clustering relative to the pristine alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The maximum He bubble size in Hf1Ta HEA can reach more than 16 nm with average sizes of 10.5 and 13.7 nm at different fluences, which was conducive to enhancing the interaction between He bubbles and dislocations and improving the hardness. Thus, the formation of large He bubbles in the irradiated Hf1Ta HEA could be considered as the main cause of hardening. Compared with the sample irradiated at low fluence, the larger and denser He bubbles generated in the sample irradiated at high fluence can interact with the dislocations more effectively, which led to the higher hardness increment and hardening fraction in the Hf1Ta HEA irradiated at the fluence of 3 × 1016 ions/cm2. Additionally, Zhao [] and Shi [] proposed that residual density of vacancies and interstitials produced by irradiation could be greatly reduced by the effective recombination in the HEAs. The severe lattice distortion in HEAs could impose restrictions on the formation and growth of defect clusters, resulting in small size defects with low density in the matrix. The HEAs are also resistant to forming large defect clusters compared with binary nickel alloy systems and have the self-healing effect. Dislocation loops and lines can significantly affect the hardening and embrittlement, but in CrMnFeCoNi and CrFeCoNi, the density of dislocation loops after irradiation by Ni ions was higher than that of binary and ternary nickel alloys, and most of these loops had a smaller size []. The reasons for the self-healing of HEAs include high atomic stress and lattice distortion caused by the large difference in atomic size, which lead to the amorphization followed by crystallization of the alloy [,], and the similarity of vacancy and interstitial migration energies, which improve the defect annihilation []. Thus, the structural features of the HEAs affect the radiation resistance.

cited_evidence.text: Table 2 shows that in CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi samples after irradiation with Kr14+ and He2+ ions, relatively small (less than 6%) concentration variations emerged. In this case, Kr irradiation alone results in a slight increase in the concentration of Fe for the CoCrFeNi HEA and the concentrations of Fe and Ni for the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The concentrations of the remaining elements decrease. Subsequent helium irradiation raises the concentrations of Co and Ni for the CoCrFeNi HEA and those of Co and Cr for the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. Relatively large variations in the concentration of elements in the samples after irradiation could be due to the migration of radiation-induced vacancies and their aggregation with helium atoms as well as the features of the HIRBS technique. Nevertheless, irradiated alloys preserve their near-equiatomic concentrations, which is mostly homogeneous apart from small redistribution of elements in the penetration layer of krypton and helium ions throughout the depth measured by HIRBS (Figure 2), and thus HEAs seem to successfully withstand radiation-stimulated segregation.
